reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A persistent, late-onset movement disorder of inner restlessness and a compelling urge to move, developing after prolonged exposure to dopamine-receptor-blocking agents and continuing well after acute akathisia would be expected to settle.
Distinguished from acute akathisia by its delayed emergence, chronicity, and tendency to persist or worsen when the offending drug is reduced or withdrawn, rather than on initiation or dose increase.

The subjective distress (tension, dysphoria, inability to keep still) is often more prominent than in tardive dyskinesia and can be mistaken for anxiety, agitation or worsening of the underlying psychiatric illness.
Characteristic motor features include marching on the spot, shifting weight, crossing and uncrossing legs, truncal rocking and inability to remain seated.
It frequently coexists with tardive dyskinesia and tardive dystonia, and complex stereotypic leg movements may blur the boundary between restlessness and dyskinesia.
Increasing the causative antipsychotic may transiently suppress symptoms (masking), reinforcing a cycle of escalating exposure; the diagnosis requires a careful temporal drug history.
Recognised because of its strong association with dysphoria, impulsivity and heightened suicide risk, warranting proactive mood and safety assessment.

Management centres on reviewing the need for and dose of the dopamine blocker, considering a switch to an agent with lower liability, and specific pharmacological strategies including VMAT2 inhibitors and, in selected cases, beta-adrenergic blockade.
reference.pathophysiology: Tardive akathisia is attributed to chronic postsynaptic dopamine D2-receptor blockade producing receptor supersensitivity and dysregulation of mesocortical, mesolimbic and nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathways that subserve motor drive and reward. Imbalance between dopaminergic and noradrenergic tone, and altered signalling in ventral striatal and limbic circuits, is thought to generate both the subjective restlessness and the semi-voluntary movements. As with other tardive syndromes, cumulative and high-potency drug exposure, and individual genetic and neurochemical vulnerability, shape the risk and persistence.
additionalDifferentials: psychomotor agitation of the underlying psychiatric disorder
restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements
tardive dyskinesia with stereotypic leg movements
additionalInvestigations: structured temporal history of all dopamine-blocking agents including antiemetics and any recent dose changes
standardised assessment with the Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale for severity and monitoring
mood, impulsivity and suicide-risk evaluation given the recognised association
screening for restless legs syndrome including iron studies where the history overlaps
thyroid function tests to exclude a metabolic driver of restlessness
review for coexisting tardive dyskinesia, dystonia or parkinsonism on examination
redFlags: emergent suicidal ideation, severe dysphoria or impulsive behaviour
escalating distress prompting inappropriate increases in the causative drug
features suggesting an evolving neuroleptic malignant syndrome such as rigidity, fever and autonomic instability
profound functional impairment or inability to rest and sleep
reference.prognosis: Tardive akathisia is often chronic and may persist for years, and can worsen transiently on withdrawal of the causative agent; some patients improve gradually once the offending drug is stopped or switched. The associated dysphoria and suicide risk make early recognition clinically important.
pitfalls: misattributing the restlessness to worsening psychosis, anxiety or agitation and escalating the antipsychotic dose
overlooking the heightened suicide and impulsivity risk associated with the disorder
failing to distinguish tardive from acute akathisia by ignoring the temporal relationship to drug changes
missing coexisting restless legs syndrome that may respond to iron repletion or dopaminergic strategies
not recognising covert dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide as the responsible agent
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition
Fahn and Jankovic, Principles and Practice of Movement Disorders, current edition
management: Review and, where clinically safe, gradually withdraw or reduce the causative dopamine-blocking agent, avoiding dose increases that merely mask symptoms
Where antipsychotic treatment must continue, switch to a lower-potency agent or to clozapine
Consider a VMAT2 inhibitor such as valbenazine, deutetrabenazine or tetrabenazine to suppress the movement disorder
Trial adjuncts such as a beta-blocker or clonidine for the subjective restlessness
Discontinue offending antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine and use non-dopaminergic alternatives
Assess and manage the associated dysphoria and suicide risk, treating comorbid mood symptoms
Monitor severity with a structured akathisia rating scale over time
Manage jointly with neurology and psychiatry
